Bellman Language Models

Adarsh Vatsa    William Eiers
Abstract

A general observation in agentic workflows, especially bounded ones, is that the decision space of the LLM, when we separate a decision from generation, starts approaching saturation: the agent meets the same states again and again, and after enough conversations it stops meeting new ones. LLMs generally don’t treat these decisions as an optimization problem and instead re-derive them from their context/prompt on every turn. We show that treating decision making within reasonable bounds as an optimization problem, solving it once, and reusing the solved decisions can often make an agent faster, cheaper and more reliable. Our approach, which we call Discretize, Then Decide, starts from data such as the workflow’s own logs or, when none exists, runs of the LLM agent itself. It reads each conversation into discrete states and estimates the probability of each outcome and the cost of each move, until no new states appear and the probabilities stop changing. It then solves the resulting Markov decision process. The solution runs as a controller around the model, sending moves whose content is fixed in the state, such as a tool call or a templated reply, and any state it hasn’t seen is sent back to the LLM. We call an LLM run this way a Bellman language model (BLM), after Richard Bellman’s equation for the best move in each state.

On τ2\tau^{2}-bench telecom, the controller with no model solves 79% of tasks. As a BLM, Qwen3.8-27B, an open model, goes from 29% to 96% with 93% fewer model calls. For Claude Opus 5.5, which solves 96% of tasks on its own, running it as a BLM cuts model calls and cost per task by about 98% and lets it solve 2 more tasks. On InventoryBench, the solved policy with no model beats every published method. Where the hard part is writing content rather than choosing moves, such as resolving SymPy issues, few decisions can be solved in advance, and a BLM helps little.

1  Introduction

A general observation about LLM agents in bounded workflows is that, once we separate a decision from the generated text used to carry it out, the space of decisions saturates. The agent meets the same states again and again, and after enough conversations it stops meeting new ones.

For example, take an agent on τ2\tau^{2}-bench’s telecom domain (Barres et al., 2026) helping a customer who can’t send picture messages. A fault is something wrong with the phone or the line that stops picture messages, such as airplane mode left on. A check is a question or instruction to the customer that finds out whether one fault is there, such as asking them to look for the airplane icon.

The agent’s replies differ in every conversation, but its decision at each turn is one of a short list. It can look up the account, run one of its checks, fix a fault, take a payment, hand the customer to a human, or close. That’s what we mean by a bounded workflow: its moves can be listed.

To choose its next move, the agent needs only a handful of facts. What’s the problem, and is it fixed yet? Is anything stopping a fix, such as a locked SIM card? Which checks are left to try? We call each combination of these facts a state.

The replies keep changing, but the states don’t. Almost every conversation we collected has messages the agent never sent before, yet on new tasks it almost never meets a state it hasn’t met before (Figure 8). One might think that just means the states keep too few facts. But in telecom they keep enough to decide well: a controller deciding from these facts alone, with no model, completes most tasks (Section 6). So the states have to keep exactly what the decision depends on.

Yet LLM agents generally don’t treat these decisions as an optimization problem. They re-derive each one from their context on every turn, with a new call to the model, so they pay for the same decisions over and over.

They also don’t always decide well. Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026) tends to ask about faults that never occur before the most common one. Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026), an open-weights model, mostly fails by handing the customer to a human while there are still checks to try. This isn’t for lack of information. In a simulated coding task where we know the true probabilities, we asked an LLM to estimate them and solved the optimization problem with its estimates. The decisions were as good as with the true probabilities, while the LLM choosing for itself did worse (Section 6).

Decisions that recur like these are what operations research learned to solve. Ordering stock, for example, became a problem with a stated cost of ordering and a stated cost of running out, solved once and applied to every order (Arrow et al., 1951). Dynamic programming did the same for sequences of decisions (Bellman, 1957). Earlier dialogue systems brought this approach to conversations, planning each move with a partially observable Markov decision process (Williams and Young, 2007; Young et al., 2013). But they understood users only through narrow, error-prone components, and mostly replied from templates. LLMs do both well.

So solving recurring decisions once isn’t new. What, then, is the contribution of this paper? We show that the idea holds up for LLM agents, and we make it work with them. For people who build agents, that’s a recipe that starts from the agent’s own logs (Section 8). For people who study them, it’s evidence that their decisions recur, and that they don’t optimize them.

The key idea is to treat an agent’s recurring decisions as an optimization problem: solve it once from data, then reuse the solution instead of re-deriving each decision on every turn. We call this method Discretize, Then Decide. It starts from the workflow’s logs, or runs of the LLM agent. As the top of Figure 1 shows, it reads each conversation into discrete states with simple rules, such as regular expressions over messages and tool results. In practice, the rules can be simple, because they only look for the handful of facts the decisions depend on. Whatever they can’t read goes to the LLM.

It then estimates, for each move, the probability of each outcome and the move’s cost, adding runs until no new states appear and the estimates stop changing. It solves the resulting Markov decision process for the lowest expected cost. The solution, the solved policy, says which move to make in each state. Whoever runs the agent chooses the unit of cost, such as customer turns in a support conversation. Every move and every outcome has a price in that unit.

The solution runs as a controller around the model. The controller reads every message and tool result into the state. When the state fixes what to send, such as an account lookup or a templated instruction, the controller sends it.

Any other turn, including every turn in a state it hasn’t seen, goes to the LLM with the task’s prompt and the conversation so far. Crucially, the model is never called on the turns the solved policy decides. We call an LLM run this way a Bellman language model (BLM), after Richard Bellman’s equation for the best move in each state (Bellman, 1957). Discretize, Then Decide is how we build one.

This differs from the usual ways of making agents cheaper or more reliable. Routers and cascades choose which model answers each query (Chen et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025), while a BLM decides whether a turn needs a model at all. Couldn’t we just write the solved policy into the prompt? Then the model still decides every turn (Xiao et al., 2024). In our experiments that makes the model more accurate than on its own, but no more efficient. Executing the solved policy does better on both (bottom of Figure 1).

Other systems carry out or enforce a written policy (Bocklisch et al., 2024; Rebedea et al., 2023; Kang et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026a), or have a model write the agent’s program, or compile its tasks or past runs into code (Qi et al., 2026; Winston et al., 2026; AgentJIT Team, 2026). Either way, a person or a model wrote the decisions. In our experiments a coding agent wrote each BLM’s rules, templates and solver too. It worked from the workflow’s guide, tools and logs (Section 3.10). But no one writes its decisions: the solver, a standard algorithm such as dynamic programming, picks the best move from estimated probabilities and stated costs, as Section 9 explains.

We evaluate BLMs in four domains, chosen to range from nearly all decisions to nearly all content. They are troubleshooting customers’ phones in τ2\tau^{2}-bench’s telecom domain, ordering stock under uncertain demand and delivery in InventoryBench (Baek et al., 2026), triaging failed test jobs in Mozilla’s continuous integration (CI), and resolving SymPy issues. The LLMs are Qwen3.8-27B and Claude Opus 5.5.

In telecom we built the controller three times, each time fixing what the last test showed. We built each from training tasks only, froze it, and then drew its own test tasks at random from the rest. We report them separately, and Appendix A lists every test, each recorded publicly before any result.

In telecom, the controller with no model at all solves most tasks. On a turn where its state doesn’t fix the move, it just sends one fixed request and reads the reply. With Qwen3.8-27B writing those turns, it solves about as many tasks as Claude Opus 5.5 alone, with far fewer model calls. Fine-tuning Qwen3.8-27B on Opus’s own conversations instead makes it solve fewer tasks than the BLM does, and it still calls the model on every turn. With Opus writing those turns, the BLM removes almost all model calls, cost and waiting time, and solves slightly more (bottom of Figure 1).

On one set of tasks, each with a fault that never appeared in the training data, we ran every task three times. As a Bellman model, Qwen3.8-27B solves nearly all of them on all three attempts, against fewer than half on its own.

How does it handle a fault it never saw? The checks come from the workflow’s own guide, not from the data. So the check for a new fault is still on the list, just last, because its fault never occurred in training. The state isn’t new either. It holds the kind of problem, whether it’s fixed yet and which checks are left, not the fault.

When the whole task is deciding, the solved policy needs little or no model. In inventory control it needs none, and it beats every published method. In test triage it pays an LLM only to read some logs, and the evidence is weaker. There it costs about as much as a fixed rule that reruns a failed test once and then escalates.

Where the hard part is writing content rather than choosing moves, as in resolving SymPy issues, few of the agent’s turns are decisions a state can fix. So a BLM helps little. The agent’s own logs show this before anyone builds a BLM. Replaying a draft controller over them shows how many of the agent’s turns its state would fix. That’s nearly all of Opus’s turns in telecom, against a small share of the SymPy agent’s turns.

The paper makes four claims:

  1. 1.

    Saturation. Once we separate deciding from writing, a bounded workflow’s states saturate, and the text doesn’t. We show this in telecom (Observation 1).

  2. 2.

    Optimality. LLM agents generally don’t optimize their decisions: a solver given the probabilities they state decides better (Observation 2).

  3. 3.

    Execution. Executing the solved decisions removes the model calls they would cost. Where most of the work is deciding, that removes most of the agent’s cost and waiting time, and its accuracy and consistency hold or improve. The gain comes from executing, not from telling the model (Observations 3 to 7).

  4. 4.

    Prediction. The agent’s own logs predict where this pays (Observation 8).

If these claims hold, an agent doesn’t have to pay again for states it has met before. Our strongest evidence comes from telecom, where LLMs play the customers, who may vary less than real ones. The other three domains show how far the claims carry, but there we kept test data apart from development less strictly (Section 5.3). Choosing the states is itself an optimization problem, and it isn’t the one we solve. When we call a decision optimal, we mean optimal for the states we chose, and Section 11 leaves the best choice of states open.

2  Preliminaries

This section sets out the agent’s world in simple terms: first in general, then in telecom, and then the decision problem they share.

In general, an LLM agent in a bounded workflow works through tasks. Each task is one instance of the same job. For example, it can be a support case, a failed test job, a stretch of weeks of ordering stock, or an issue to fix in a code base. On each turn it makes one move from a short list. Some moves gather information, such as a lookup or a question. Some act, such as a fix, an order or an edit. And some end the task, such as closing it or handing it to a person.

Some of what matters stays hidden from the agent, such as which faults a phone has, or whether a failed test is a real regression. The workflow usually comes with written rules about what the agent may do, and every move has a cost, in one unit that whoever deploys the agent cares about.

Concretely, in telecom, each task is one support case. A customer can’t do something with their phone, such as send picture messages, because something on the phone or the line is wrong. Each such problem is a fault: airplane mode left on, roaming off while the customer is abroad, or the network set to 2G only. A case can have several faults at once, and it’s solved only when all of them are fixed.

The agent and the customer take turns. A check asks the customer to look at one setting, such as whether airplane mode is on, to find out whether its fault is there. If it is, the check also asks them to change the setting. Some faults also need a fix on the account, made with a tool call, such as enabling roaming on the line. The agent can also look up the account, the line or the bill, close the conversation, or hand the customer to a human, which we call a hand-off.

In telecom, the benchmark gives the agent two documents. The troubleshooting guide lists the checks in three stages: the line’s service, then mobile data, then picture messaging. The written policy sets rules the agent has to follow, such as allowing a hand-off when the SIM card is locked. Some of its rules are procedures, fixed series of steps, such as taking a payment before resuming a suspended line.

Telecom has the shape of troubleshooting: the hidden facts are faults, the information moves are checks, and each check also fixes what it finds. Other workflows fill the same parts differently.

In continuous integration, the hidden fact is whether a failed test job is a real regression or an intermittent failure. The information moves are rerunning the job and paying an LLM to read its error lines. Each task ends by marking the failure intermittent, backing out the change, or escalating to a person.

In inventory control there’s nothing to ask: news about demand and deliveries arrives on its own, and the only move is how much to order. In SymPy, the hidden fact is which phase of its work the coding agent is in, and the information moves are searching, reading and running code. Most of the work is the agent’s own edits. Table 7, in Appendix E, gives each domain’s parts.

Which move should come next? That’s a decision problem with three parts: the states a task can be in, the moves available in each, and what each move costs and leads to. In telecom, a state holds the four facts from the introduction: the kind of problem, whether it’s fixed yet, anything stopping a fix, and which checks are left.

A policy says which move to make in each state. The solved policy is the best one we can compute from the estimates, with the lowest expected total cost. We compute it once, before any conversation. A controller then sends its moves, as tool calls or templated messages, and the LLM writes everything else.

So a BLM saves in two ways. What the solved policy minimizes depends on the workflow: customer turns in telecom, dollars in CI, tokens in SymPy. And every move the controller sends costs no model call at all, whatever the solved policy minimizes. That second saving is the one our experiments show most clearly: in telecom, the BLMs removed 93 to 98% of the model calls (Section 6). We build each of these up step by step in Section 3, and write them down formally in Section 3.6.

It’s tempting to read “bounded” as “small”. It isn’t. A workflow is bounded when we can list its moves and read the facts its decisions depend on, however many there are. Picture an airline rebooking thousands of passengers after a storm, or a hospital assigning beds and staff through the night. Or picture a warehouse deciding what to pick and restock, or a cloud provider working incidents across thousands of services. Each has a finite menu of moves, facts we can read, and decisions that come back again and again.

Their state spaces are huge, but solving large decision problems is what modern compute does well, and we have to do it only once. So we can generally put decision making in bounded environments into this shape, and leave the LLM to handle the language and whatever the controller hasn’t seen before. What limits it isn’t the size of the environment, but whether its states repeat often enough and whether we can observe its outcomes (Section 4).

3  Discretize, Then Decide

How can an agent stop re-deriving decisions it has met before? Read its conversations into discrete states, and solve the resulting decision problem once. A controller can then make those decisions on every turn without calling the model, and send every state it hasn’t seen back to the LLM.

This section builds a Bellman model on a simpler version of one task, one step at a time. Then we state the decision problem in general, give the algorithm, and show what changes for the real telecom controller.

3.1  A worked example

Take the customer from the introduction, who can’t send picture messages. In our worked example, only three things can be wrong, alone or together. Concretely, the customer may be abroad with roaming off on the line, the phone may be in airplane mode, or its network mode preference may be set to 2G only. For each fault the agent has one check, which finds the fault and fixes it. The agent can also hand the customer to a human, or close once the customer says picture messages work.

These three faults come from a real task in our test set, which Section 3.8 returns to. The real workflow has lookups and 14 checks, which the troubleshooting guide sorts into three stages. We keep just enough in the example to follow each step by hand.

3.2  Step 1: read each conversation into discrete states

An agent’s replies differ in every conversation, but what its next move depends on is small. In the example, it’s which checks the agent has made, what the customer reported, and whether picture messages work yet. We call each combination of these facts a state. A BLM reads every message into the state with simple rules, which we call the reader. It reads the agent’s own messages too, to know which checks the agent has made.

As Figure 2 shows, customers say they’re abroad in many ways, but the reader keeps only the fact that they’re abroad. The wording is gone, so different conversations end up in the same state. However a conversation goes, it’s always in one of a few states, and the agent meets the same states again and again.

3.3  Step 2: estimate the probability of each outcome and the cost of each move

Next, we count. For a check, the outcome that matters is whether it finds a fault. Figure 3 shows eight past tasks, each with the faults it really had, much as a support center’s closed tickets record what was wrong. For example, roaming was off for a customer abroad in six of the eight, so the probability of that fault is 0.75. Airplane mode and the 2G-only setting each appear in four, so theirs are 0.5.

The cost of a check is the number of customer turns it takes. In the example, asking about travel takes one turn, and so does checking airplane mode. The network mode takes two. In the real workflow we measure turns in logged conversations, and we keep adding conversations until no new states appear and the probabilities stop changing.

3.4  Step 3: solve once, before any conversation

Which check should come first? One might start with the most likely fault, or with the check that takes the fewest turns. The solved policy combines the two. It asks first about the fault with the highest probability per turn, the classical rule for ordering tests (Kadane and Simon, 1977). Travel comes first at 0.75 per turn, then airplane mode at 0.5, then the network mode at 0.25. The rule is exact when there’s one fault to find. With several at once it’s an approximation, but here it still picks the best of the six orders (Figure 4).

Is this order really the best? Here we can check, because there are only six ways to order three checks. A conversation ends as soon as the last of the customer’s faults is gone, so a task costs the turns of every check up to that point.

Take the three customers with roaming as their only fault. Asking about travel first ends each of their conversations after one turn. Asking about it last makes them sit through the other two checks first, four turns each. The two-turn network check gains from going last, too: only the four customers with that fault ever pay for it. Added up over the eight past tasks, the solved order takes 21 customer turns, and the other five orders take 22 to 30 (Figure 4, right). These are totals. A single customer never needs more than four turns, the cost of all three checks.

An agent that never asks about travel does worse still. It can’t fix six of the eight tasks, which is the mistake Qwen alone made on the real task (Section 3.8). Even so, it turns out that the order itself matters less than this example suggests. In the real telecom workflow, success comes from making every check, in almost any order (Section 7). What pays is that the solved policy is computed once, before any conversation, so the next step can carry it out without a model.

3.5  Step 4: run the solution as a controller around the model

In Figure 5, we run the solved policy on a new customer who has all three faults. On every turn, the controller reads the latest message into the state. If the state fixes what to send, the controller sends it without calling the model. We call such a turn covered. The controller may send a templated question, an instruction, or a tool call, such as enabling roaming on the line.

When the customer says something no rule reads, such as asking where to find a setting, the turn is uncovered and goes to the LLM. Notice that the model itself doesn’t change. It gets the task’s own prompt, its tools and the whole conversation so far. The controller sends the LLM’s reply and reads it back into the state, so it can take over again on the next turn.

In this conversation, the LLM writes one of the five replies, and the checks take four customer turns, as Figure 4 counts them. That’s a BLM’s main saving: the other four replies cost no model call.

Because every uncovered turn goes to the LLM, the solved policy doesn’t have to cover every state. It only has to be right about the turns it covers.

The controller also looks at what the LLM sends. Suppose the model tries to hand the customer to a human while checks remain and nothing is stopping a fix, as a locked SIM card would. The controller doesn’t send the hand-off. It asks the model again, listing the checks not yet made, at most three times per conversation. After that, the hand-off goes through.

Executing the moves, rather than suggesting them, matters. When our SymPy controller only suggested when the coding agent should stop, the agent followed 6.5% of the suggestions.

3.6  The decision problem

Here is the decision problem a BLM solves, stated precisely. The state of Section 2 is the observed state xx: discrete fields read from messages and tool results. Some things that matter can’t be read directly, such as which faults are still present on the phone. We call these the hidden state hh. The controller keeps a belief bb, a probability for each value of hh.

A move aa costs c⁡(x,h,a)c(x,h,a). Some moves gather information, such as a lookup, a check or a second run of a failed test job. Some act, such as a fix or an order. Some end the task, such as closing or a hand-off to a person. After each move, the reader turns what comes back into an observation oo, which occurs with probability P⁡(o∣x,h,a)P(o\mid x,h,a).

Choosing moves to minimize the expected total cost then becomes a partially observable Markov decision process (Kaelbling et al., 1998). When nothing that matters is hidden, it’s a Markov decision process. A solution is a solved policy π⁡(x,b)↦a\pi(x,b)\mapsto a, stored as a table or computed by a small search at run time. In the worked example, for instance, xx holds the checks made and the customer’s reports, and hh is the set of faults still present. Each move costs the customer turns it takes, and the solved policy is the order of Figure 4.

Whoever deploys the agent chooses what the solved policy minimizes, not the model. We price every move and every outcome in one unit, and the solved policy minimizes the expected total. In telecom the unit is customer turns, so the solved policy asks first where a fault is most likely per turn spent. Minimizing turns can’t make it give up early. It closes only once the customer reports the problem fixed. It hands the customer to a human only when the written policy says to, as for a locked SIM card.

Other domains use other units. In continuous integration it’s dollars, from runner prices and developer time. In InventoryBench it’s the benchmark’s reward, the margin on sales minus the cost of holding stock. In SymPy it’s billed tokens. A different unit gives a different solved policy from the same probabilities. If every check took the same number of turns, the order would follow the probabilities alone.

The unit can be time, too. When speed is what matters, price each move in minutes or turns, as telecom does with customer turns. A hard time limit doesn’t add up move by move, so it goes into the state as the time left, or becomes a limit on the expected total (Altman, 1999). Whatever the unit, the moves the controller sends cost no model call. So the saving in model calls, and in what they cost, comes from executing the solved policy, not from what it minimizes (Section 4.5).

Three conditions make this work. We can list the moves. We can observe the outcomes that matter, so we can estimate their probabilities. And a finite set of states is enough to tell apart the conversations that need different moves.

The third condition is where saturation comes in, and it depends on choosing the state well. The state has to keep what the decision depends on, not the whole conversation. In the worked example, the checks made can come in only eight combinations. In telecom, with 14 checks, the record of checks made keeps growing, because LLM agents try checks in new combinations.

But the state the solved policy acts on stops growing (Observation 1). In telecom, the solved policy makes the checks in a fixed order. So it doesn’t need the whole record of checks made, only the first check in that order not yet made. Its state holds that check, the kind of problem, whether it’s fixed yet, and anything stopping a fix. Section 4 makes the third condition precise and bounds what it costs when it holds only approximately.

3.7  The algorithm

Algorithm 1 builds the solved policy once, and Algorithm 2 runs it on every turn. Together they’re the four steps above, written for any workflow.

Algorithm 1 stops collecting when new conversations stop adding states and the estimated probabilities stop moving. Section 4.3 turns this test into a number, and Section 3.8 shows how we chose the data for the telecom controller. Algorithm 2 reads every turn into the state, including the turns the LLM writes, so the controller always knows where the conversation stands.

Algorithm 3 looks similar to Algorithm 2, since both have the solved policy. The difference is where the decision happens. In Algorithm 3 the model still reads the conversation and decides on every turn. So every turn is still a model call, and it’s up to the model whether to follow the solved policy. We test this alternative at three levels of detail (Section 5.2), and Observation 6 compares it with executing the solved policy.

3.8  Building the telecom controller

The three faults of the worked example come from a real task in our test set, which we picked as an example. Section 6 gives the rates over all tasks. Figure 6 sets two conversations on this one side by side. On the left, Qwen3.8-27B runs the benchmark’s own agent. On the right, the same LLM runs as a Bellman model. The simulated customer is the same in both.

Both agents found the airplane mode, and Qwen alone even fixed the network mode, which the Bellman model reached only later. But Qwen alone never asked whether the customer was traveling. After checking everything else it could think of, it told the customer it had run out of standard troubleshooting steps, and handed them to a human. The BLM asked about travel third, enabled roaming itself with one tool call, and finished the task without calling the model once.

Why third, and not first as in the worked example? In short, because the guide puts two other checks in an earlier stage. The rest of this subsection follows Algorithm 1 for the controller behind the right-hand column, the last of the three we built for telecom, and says what changes from the example.

Before building anything, we split the benchmark’s 2,285 tasks once (Section 5.3). The probabilities and the costs below come only from the 1,175 training tasks. Each task is a customer with a known set of faults, as in the worked example.

We used two kinds of data. The first is the tasks themselves, which for picture messaging are 1,013 cases, each with its faults. The second is conversations on training tasks. Claude Opus 5.5 ran on its own on 400 of them. These were 238 picture-messaging tasks, and every task of the benchmark’s two other kinds of problem, a phone with no service and one with no mobile data. Qwen3.8-27B had 1,321 conversations (Appendix H).

In practice, the real reader has more to read than the example’s. From the customer’s first message it reads the kind of problem. From each later message, it reads whether the problem is fixed yet and what the customer reports about each setting. From the agent’s own messages, it reads which check the agent asked for, and from the customer’s reports and the account lookups, anything stopping a fix. The coding agent wrote the rules from the benchmark’s troubleshooting guide and what the phone displays, and corrected them on training conversations and on the failures of earlier controllers.

Measured against logs the agent never sees, the reader identified the kind of problem in 1,717 of 1,721 training conversations and whether it was fixed yet on 95.7% of turns. It found the checks actually made with a precision of 0.90 and a recall of 0.875.

The probabilities are counts, as in the worked example. Roaming is off while the customer is abroad in 750 of the 1,013 picture-messaging tasks, so its probability is 0.74. The VPN fault occurs in none, so its probability is 0. The other two solvers we compare (Section 5.2) also count how often each combination of faults occurs. They update these probabilities after every reply by Bayes’ rule, with a fixed allowance for misreading the customer.

The turns come from Opus’s conversations. A check’s cost is the number of customer turns from the one where Opus first asked about it to the one where it asked about the next. We averaged this over the 229 solved conversations among the first 233 to finish. Asking about travel took 1.20 turns, and the SIM card took 2.86.

Solving is the same sort as in the worked example, with one change. The guide orders the checks in three stages: the line’s service, then mobile data, then picture messaging. Within each stage, the solved policy asks first about the fault with the highest probability per turn. Checks for faults that never occur come last.

Roaming has the highest probability per turn, but comes third (Table 1). Airplane mode and the SIM card come first, because they belong to the first stage. That’s why the BLM asked about travel third. The turn counts come from Opus’s own conversations, yet Opus orders the checks differently, and asks about travel only after seven other checks.

Last, each check gets one fixed instruction, and each fault one fixed way to fix it. The account lookups and the written policy’s procedures become tool calls, such as enabling roaming for a customer abroad or taking a payment before resuming a suspended line. The controller reads their arguments from the state. These are written once, from the written policy, the guide and the tools.

In our experiments, we fixed the training data in advance rather than collecting it until nothing new appeared. Measured afterwards, the states in them had saturated (Observation 1).

3.9  Running the controller, with and without an LLM

In the conversation of Figure 6, the state fixed what to send on every turn. So the controller sent every message, and the model was never called. Appendix F follows that conversation turn by turn, from the controller’s side.

A turn is uncovered when the state doesn’t fix what to send, as when the customer asks something off-script or answers in a way no rule reads. In the worked example, such a turn went to the LLM, and that’s one of two ways we run a BLM. Without an LLM, the controller sends one fixed request instead. It asks, “Could you please tell me what you see on your phone right now, so I can help you with the next step?” It then reads the reply like any other.

3.10  Implementation

Other domains read their states in other ways. For SymPy issues, a small fine-tuned classifier, Laya (Convai Innovations, 2026), reads which phase of its work the coding agent is in. In continuous integration and inventory control, every field of the state comes from the system exactly. Appendix E gives the state, the probabilities, the costs and the solvers of each domain.

Where data are thin, we can start from an LLM’s own estimates of the probabilities and let the counts correct them. The LLM’s guess then counts like a fixed number of past tasks (Section 8).

The controllers are 300 to 1,250 lines of Python per domain. They were written by an AI coding agent, Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5, under our direction. It read each benchmark’s instructions, tools and development logs. It wrote the readers, templates and solvers, and worked out from the logs why runs failed. Section 10.1 gives the point at which building one pays for itself. At run time, a step of the telecom controller takes about 66 microseconds, timed on an earlier version.

4  What solving once guarantees

Section 3 described how we build and run a BLM. What does it guarantee, and at what cost? Each result comes with its intuition, and proofs are in Appendix B.

4.1  Optimality for the estimates

Once we write down the probabilities and the costs, finding the best moves is a solved problem. Dynamic programming finds the solved policy, the one with the least expected total cost under those estimates.

Two design rules keep the problem well posed. Costs must add over steps, so anything that doesn’t add, such as a shared budget, goes into the state. And every task must be able to end, and not ending must cost something. So each state offers a move that ends the task, such as closing or a hand-off, and every other move has a positive cost, or a step limit ends any loop.

Proposition 1 (The solved policy is optimal for the estimates).

If the states carry everything the decision depends on, costs add over steps, some policy ends the task with probability one from every state, and any policy that never ends it has infinite expected cost, then value iteration over the estimated decision process converges to the optimal costs-to-go, and choosing in each state the move with the lowest cost-to-go gives a policy of least expected total cost for that process (Bellman, 1957; Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis, 1991).

With a hidden state, the beliefs themselves form a decision process (Kaelbling et al., 1998), which we solve approximately, in three ways that Section 5.2 describes and Section 7 compares. Proposition 1 says nothing about how well our estimates match the world. The next results bound the two ways it can fall short: states that group too much together, and estimates that are off.

4.2  The cost of discretizing

A decision state groups many conversations together. In telecom, conversations that made different checks, in different orders, can share a decision state. They only have to agree on the kind of problem, whether it’s fixed yet, anything stopping a fix, and the first check in the solved order not yet made. Grouping throws information away, and what we lose depends on how differently the grouped conversations would score each move. To state this, call everything about a conversation so far its full state ss. Write Q⋆​(s,a)Q^{\star}(s,a) for the least expected cost of finishing the task after taking move aa in ss.

Proposition 2 (Discretizing costs at most 2​ε2\varepsilon per decision).

For full states that meet the conditions of Proposition 1, call a grouping of them into decision states ε\varepsilon-consistent if any two full states s,s′s,s^{\prime} in the same decision state satisfy |Q⋆​(s,a)−Q⋆​(s′,a)|≤ε|Q^{\star}(s,a)-Q^{\star}(s^{\prime},a)|\leq\varepsilon for every move aa. Let π\pi choose, in each decision state, a move that minimizes some weighted average of Q⋆​(s,⋅)Q^{\star}(s,\cdot) over the full states it groups. Then from any start state s0s_{0}, Vπ​(s0)≤V⋆​(s0)+2​ε​𝔼π​[T]V^{\pi}(s_{0})\leq V^{\star}(s_{0})+2\varepsilon\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[T], where VπV^{\pi} and V⋆V^{\star} are the expected costs of following π\pi and of acting optimally, and TT is the number of decisions π\pi makes.

The proof uses the performance difference lemma (Kakade and Langford, 2002). Proposition 2 lets us trade ε\varepsilon against savings. Grouping more gives a smaller solved policy and larger savings, at a loss that grows linearly in ε\varepsilon and in the length of the task. Solving the grouped model directly is exact at ε=0\varepsilon=0 (Li et al., 2006) and loses an amount linear in ε\varepsilon otherwise (Abel et al., 2016).

The proposition also suggests a rule for finding decision states from data. When the conversations grouped into one state keep needing different moves, the state groups too much: split it, as utile distinctions do (McCallum, 1995). When two states never lead to different moves, merge them. Stop when neither happens.

4.3  When to stop collecting data

Algorithm 1 adds runs until no new states appear and the estimates stop changing. We can make both parts of this test precise, the first here and the second in the next subsection.

For new states, suppose the last nn conversations added no new decision state, and future conversations come from the same distribution as the collected ones. Then, with 95% confidence, fewer than a share 3/n3/n of future conversations will reach a decision state not seen so far: this is the rule of three (Hanley and Lippman-Hand, 1983). Those conversations fall back to the LLM.

So if we accept that a share pp of conversations reach an unseen state, we can stop after 3/p3/p conversations without a new one, for example 150 conversations for p=2%p=2\%. Observation 1 applies the rule to telecom. The rule assumes that nn is fixed in advance, so when it’s applied after every conversation, its 95% level is approximate. It also says nothing about a shift in the kind of task arriving. When the mix of tasks changes, the count starts again.

For the estimates, the next result shows that only one kind of change matters: a change large enough to flip a decision.

4.4  How precise the estimates need to be

An estimate matters only if it changes a decision. If the cheapest move is the same for every probability between the estimate and the truth, an error in the estimate costs nothing.

Proposition 3 (Estimates matter only near decision thresholds).

Let Y∈{0,1}Y\in\{0,1\} be the hidden outcome, such as whether a failure is a regression, and let each move aa that ends the task have cost C⁡(a,b)=b​ca​1+(1−b)​ca​0C(a,b)=b\,c_{a1}+(1-b)\,c_{a0}, linear in b=P⁡(Y=1)b=P(Y{=}1) with slope sa=ca​1−ca​0s_{a}=c_{a1}-c_{a0}. Acting on a belief b^\hat{b} when the true probability is bb costs at most |b^−b|⋅maxa,a′⁡|sa−sa′||\hat{b}-b|\cdot\max_{a,a^{\prime}}|s_{a}-s_{a^{\prime}}| more than acting on bb, and nothing unless a decision threshold lies between them.

For example, in Mozilla’s continuous integration, a failed test job is either a regression or an intermittent failure. Marking it intermittent costs two developer-hours if it was a regression. Backing out the change costs an hour of rework if it wasn’t. Escalating to a person costs fifteen minutes either way. Once rerunning the job is no longer worth its price, the cheapest move depends only on which side of two thresholds the belief falls: 0.125 and 0.75.

Notice that an estimate of 0.3 that should have been 0.5 changes nothing. An estimate of 0.8 that should have been 0.7 backs out a change that should have been escalated (Section 7 shows this happening). So we should spend precision only near the thresholds. This is also why a solved policy can start from an LLM’s rough estimates, and why the second stopping test needs only the estimates near a threshold to stop changing.

4.5  What solving once saves

Amdahl’s law (Amdahl, 1967) says that making part of a job free can never save more than that part’s share of the work. The same holds here. The turns the controller decides become nearly free, and the turns that still go to the model set the limit. Here we count what it costs to make the decisions, in model calls, with a decision made by the model costing one call. This isn’t the cost the solved policy minimizes (Section 3.6): a solved policy that minimizes customer turns also saves model calls, because it’s executed rather than re-derived.

Let reading each turn into the state cost a fraction ρ\rho of a model call, and let a share ff of decisions fall back to the model. If we also have the model double-check some of the controller’s decisions, to catch its mistakes, let that share be aa. Finally, let building the solved policy cost BB once.

Proposition 4 (Cost law).

Over NN conversations of TT decisions each, solving once makes deciding cheaper by the factor

R=1B/N​T+ρ+f+a.R=\frac{1}{B/NT+\rho+f+a}. (1)

It pays for itself once N​T>B/(1−ρ−f−a)NT>B/(1-\rho-f-a), and RR approaches 1/(ρ+f+a)1/(\rho+f+a) as the number of conversations grows. If the solved decisions also change the number of decisions per task to T′T^{\prime}, the last three terms scale by T′/TT^{\prime}/T.

Figure 7 draws the law for a small example. Savings rise quickly with traffic and then level off at a ceiling set by the share of decisions that fall back to the model. Past that point the cost of building no longer matters, and only the fallback share still changes the savings.

That share, which plays the role of Amdahl’s serial fraction, is one we can measure before deploying the solved policy. Replay the frozen controller over an agent’s existing logs and count the turns where the controller’s state already fixes the content. We call this the decidable share, and the fallback share is roughly what’s left. Section 6 compares it with the calls the BLMs actually removed, in four domains. Section 10.1 works out the break-even point for the telecom results.

5  Four domains, from nearly all decisions to nearly all content

Where should solving once pay off? We hypothesize that how much of an agent’s work we can solve in advance depends on how much of it is choosing among recurring moves, rather than writing new content. So we chose four domains across that range. Telecom troubleshooting is mostly decisions, inventory control and test-failure triage are only decisions, and resolving SymPy issues is mostly content.

5.1  Domains

τ2\tau^{2}-bench telecom (Barres et al., 2026; Sierra Research, 2026). A simulated customer has a phone with one or more faults and a problem of one of three kinds: no service, no mobile data, or picture messages that won’t send. The agent works on the account through tools. The customer works on the phone, so the agent has to ask for every phone check. The benchmark’s own scorer judges success. The benchmark has 2,285 tasks.

InventoryBench (Baek et al., 2026). An agent orders stock each period under uncertain demand and uncertain delivery times. The benchmark has 1,320 instances built from real H&M demand and from synthetic series, in six batches (real or synthetic demand, with lead times of zero periods, four periods, or random). The score is the benchmark’s normalized reward, and published methods are on its leaderboard (InventoryBench, 2026). The controller makes no model calls here.

Mozilla CI triage (Lampel et al., 2021). Each failed test job on Mozilla’s integration branch is either a regression or an intermittent failure. The controller can retrigger the job, ask an LLM to read its error lines, mark it intermittent, back out the change, or escalate to a person. Costs are runner list prices times minutes, and developer time: fifteen minutes for an escalation, two hours for a missed regression, one hour for a backout that wasn’t needed. From 223,699 failed jobs over 120 days we sampled 5,000 with staff labels. Controllers are fitted on an earlier training window and tested on the 1,173 failures of a later window.

Scoring every method on every failure needs the outcomes of retriggers that never happened. So we report two scores: one on the 169 failures with all outcomes observed, and one on all failures, with the missing outcomes simulated. The score is dollars per failure.

SymPy issue resolution (Jimenez et al., 2024). A Qwen3.8-27B coding agent works on issues from the SymPy repository. The controller decides when the agent should run its tests and when to stop, and it carries out the submission itself. It reads the agent’s phase with the Laya classifier. We test on 21 issues, three runs each, scored by the issues’ hidden tests, with the agent’s billed tokens as cost.

Appendix E lists, for each domain, the state, the hidden variable, the reader, the moves, the cost unit and the solvers.

5.2  What we compare

We use two LLMs: Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026), an open-weights model that we run ourselves, and Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026). Unless we say otherwise, Qwen3.8-27B runs with its thinking mode off. Appendix C gives the details of how we ran each model.

The main comparison is always between an LLM agent and a Bellman model built on the same LLM. The LLM agent is the benchmark’s own agent, unchanged: the same prompt, written policy and tools. In the BLM, the controller sends the move on every turn the solved policy covers, and the same LLM writes every other turn. Note that the controller’s moves go out as ordinary messages and tool calls, so the benchmark scores both agents in exactly the same way.

Two variations of the BLM show how the work is divided. In the first there’s no LLM at all: when a turn isn’t covered, the controller simply asks the customer to describe what they see (Section 3.9). This measures what the solved policy does on its own. In the second, which we call the thinking fallback, the LLM that writes the uncovered turns uses its thinking mode.

To separate knowing the solved policy from executing it, we also give the LLM the solved policy as text, as in Algorithm 3, at three levels of detail. Concretely, the checklist gives the order of checks and the steps of each procedure. The checklist with templates adds the exact wording of every message the controller would send. The oracle plan is the benchmark’s own list of the actions each task requires. We also ran the checklist with thinking on.

We can solve the decision process in more than one way, and we compare three solvers, all using the same states, probabilities and costs. The simplest ignores the uncertainty about the hidden state. In telecom it’s the fixed order of checks in Section 3.8 (Table 1). In the other domains, it acts as if the most likely value of the hidden state were the true one.

The second, QMDP (Littman et al., 1995), scores each move under the current belief, but assumes the uncertainty will be gone after one step. The third plans over beliefs, and Appendix E gives each domain’s version. In telecom, the fixed order was the configuration we registered in advance as our main one.

In the other domains we compare against the strongest baselines we could find. In InventoryBench, these are the methods on the benchmark’s leaderboard and a published operations-research rule, which our implementation reproduces. We also ran Claude Opus 5.5 with the benchmark’s best published strategy, in which the LLM sets each order after seeing that rule’s recommendation, on 60 instances drawn at random. In CI, they’re simple rules, such as “retrigger once, then escalate”, and an LLM given the same prices and probabilities as the controller. In SymPy, the strongest simple baseline is a rule that stops the agent at its first passing test.

5.3  Test sets and registration

We split τ2\tau^{2}-telecom’s 2,285 tasks before building any controller: 1,175 for training, 495 for testing, and 501 that each contain a type of fault missing from the training tasks. We used the benchmark’s own 114 base tasks during development.

We froze each controller and recorded a hash of its code before drawing its test tasks at random with a public source of random numbers (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2018; Kelsey et al., 2019). We committed the hash, the drawn tasks and the analysis plan to a public repository within a minute of the draw, before any result. We call this record a registration. When a test showed a flaw, the fix went into a new controller, tested on newly drawn tasks, and earlier results stand. This produced five telecom test sets, which we always report separately:

  • •

    test set 1: 80 picture-messaging and 34 mobile-data tasks, for the first controller;

  • •

    test set 2: 114 picture-messaging tasks, for the second controller, which we repeated with Claude Opus 5.5 playing the customer (the registered comparison uses 64 of them);

  • •

    test set 3: 114 picture-messaging tasks, for the third controller;

  • •

    unseen-fault set 1: 60 tasks, each with a type of fault missing from all training tasks, for the first controller;

  • •

    unseen-fault set 2: 60 other such tasks, for the third controller, with Opus playing the customer and three attempts per task.

Appendix A lists every registration and its outcome, including predictions that turned out wrong.

We couldn’t test the other domains this way. In CI and SymPy, we froze the controllers before their only scoring run, but we had seen the same failures and issues while building earlier versions. InventoryBench has no separate test data, so we chose the settings for its real-demand batches using only its synthetic batches, and the other way round.

5.4  Measurements

In telecom, Qwen3.8-27B simulates the customer, except where we say that Opus plays the customer. In practice, the simulated customer’s replies vary a little from run to run even with randomness turned off, so we compare agents task by task.

We report the share of tasks solved and, where we attempted each task three times, the share solved in all three attempts, which τ2\tau^{2}-bench calls pass3 (Barres et al., 2026). For cost and speed we report:

  • •

    model calls: the agent’s LLM calls per conversation;

  • •

    tokens: what the agent’s model reads and writes, including its thinking but not the simulated customer’s;

  • •

    cost: the dollar cost of Opus’s calls at list prices;

  • •

    waiting time: the time between each customer message and the agent’s reply, added up over the conversation.

Ranges in brackets are 95% confidence intervals from resampling tasks (in CI, groups of failures from the same code change; in SymPy, issues). Section 4.5 defines the decidable share, and Appendix G describes how we measure it.

6  The states repeat, and executing the solved policy pays

Do the claims of Section 1 hold? Table 2 gives the registered telecom results, and eight observations follow, each tied to one of the claims. The other domains appear where they bear on a claim.

Observation 1: Most of a bounded workflow is recurring decisions, and the state those decisions depend on saturates. With no model at all, the solved policy solves 90 of the 114 tasks in test set 2, against 31 for Qwen3.8-27B on its own (Table 4).

Figure 8 shows why we can decide so much in advance. We replayed the 1,721 conversations on training tasks that ran without a solved policy through the controller’s reader, in the order we collected them. We counted the distinct values of three things: the decision state the solved policy acts on, the full record of which checks a conversation had made, and the agent’s messages. The decision state took 69 values, and none of the last 179 conversations added one.

The rule of three (Section 4.3) bounds the share of new conversations that would reach an unseen decision state at 1.7%. On the test sets, the share was 0.2%, 2 of 965 conversations, on 5 of their 17,438 turns.

The record of checks made kept growing, to 2,664 values, with new ones in 59 of the last 100 conversations. And 518 of the 965 test conversations reached a record not seen in training: LLM agents keep trying checks in new combinations. The agent’s messages repeated least of all, with 18,254 distinct messages and new ones in 99 of the last 100 conversations. Appendix H gives the make-up of the training conversations, the coverage of each test set, and further checks of the reader.

Observation 2: LLM agents know what they need to decide well, but they generally don’t optimize. Qwen3.8-27B’s failures are mostly hand-offs. Most of its failed conversations ended with the customer handed to a human while the solved policy still had a move to make: 49 of 62, 76 of 83 and 73 of 81 on test sets 1, 2 and 3. On test set 3, the Bellman model solved 69 of the 73 tasks Qwen lost this way.

It turns out that thinking doesn’t remove the pattern: with thinking on, Qwen solves 62 of the 114 tasks in test set 2, against 102 as a BLM with thinking off (Table 4). Opus’s order of checks doesn’t follow the fault rates in its own conversations (Table 1).

The most direct evidence comes from a simulated coding agent, where each move costs minutes of work and we know the true probabilities, so we can score every decision exactly (Appendix J). There, a solved policy computed from an LLM’s own estimates of the probabilities cost 29.9 minutes per task, the same as one computed from the true probabilities. An LLM choosing each move itself cost 32.2 to 33.0 minutes.

Observation 3: As a BLM, a small open model reaches the accuracy of a frontier model, including on faults it never saw. On test sets 1, 2 and 3, Qwen3.8-27B as a BLM solved 94, 102 and 109 of 114 tasks, against 52, 31 and 33 on its own (Table 2). Those are gains of 36.8 [27.2, 46.5], 62.3 [52.6, 71.9] and 66.7 [57.0, 75.4] points.

With the third controller, that is within one task of Claude Opus 5.5 on its own (−-0.9 points [−-6.1, 4.4]), at 1.5 model calls per conversation against Opus’s 16.9. With a thinking fallback, the BLM matched Opus at 110 tasks (0.0 [−-4.4, 4.4]), using 4.7 thousand agent tokens per conversation against Opus’s 245 thousand. The first two controllers fell short of Opus, by 14.9 and 7.9 points.

The gains held on faults the controller had never seen. In unseen-fault set 1, every task contains a type of fault missing from the training tasks, so we never estimated its probability. As a BLM, Qwen went from 22 to 42 of 60 tasks, ++33.3 points [16.7, 50.0]. The gains were largest on the tasks with the most faults, which need the most decisions (Appendix I). They also held with a stronger customer. With Opus playing the customer on 64 tasks of test set 2, Qwen went from 45 to 63 as a BLM, against a registered forecast of ++28 points (++28.1 [17.2, 40.6]).

Observation 4: For a frontier model, a BLM removes almost all model calls, cost and waiting time, without losing accuracy. With Claude Opus 5.5 as a BLM, the three test sets saw 114, 113 and 112 tasks solved, against 111, 111 and 110 for Opus on its own. Model calls per conversation fell from 15.6, 17.0 and 16.9 to 0.43, 0.61 and 0.25. The cost per conversation fell from $0.43–0.49 to $0.012–0.024. On test sets 1 and 2, the customer’s total waiting time per conversation fell from 77.8 and 87.0 seconds to 2.5 and 3.7 seconds, with a median of 0 seconds. Part of Opus’s time is the overhead of the interface we reached it through (Appendix C).

Figure 9 shows what this looks like: in 82 of the 114 conversations of test set 1, and 74 of test set 2, the BLM never called the LLM. Of the turns the controller executes, about a quarter are account lookups and a quarter to a third are checks in the solved order. A fifth are steps of procedures from the written policy. What didn’t fall is the number of customer messages. On test set 3, conversations with the BLM had 31.5 of them against 28.2 for Opus alone, because the controller asks one check per message.

Observation 5: BLMs succeed consistently across repeated attempts. A support agent that solves a task only some of the time is of limited use, which is why τ2\tau^{2}-bench reports passk. Unseen-fault set 2 tests this. Every task contains a type of fault missing from the training tasks, Opus plays the customer, and each task is attempted three times. Qwen3.8-27B on its own succeeded in 67.2% of attempts but solved only 40.0% of tasks in all three (Table 3).

As a BLM, it succeeded in 97.8% of attempts and solved 93.3% of tasks in all three, at 0.97 model calls per conversation. That’s ++30.6 points [22.8, 38.9] on attempts, the registered primary measure, and ++53.3 [41.7, 66.7] on all three. With a thinking fallback, and with Opus as a BLM, every one of the 180 attempts succeeded. To save cost, we ran Opus on its own for only 41 of its planned 180 attempts. It solved all 41, at 16.3 model calls per conversation.

Observation 6: Telling the model the solved policy improves its accuracy but not its efficiency, while executing the solved policy improves both. On test set 2 we gave Qwen3.8-27B the solved policy as text (Table 4, Figure 1). The checklist took it from 31 to 69 tasks, the checklist with every template to 99, thinking with the checklist to 103, and the benchmark’s oracle plan to 106. Every one of these still made 18 to 23 model calls per conversation, against 18.4 for Qwen on its own.

Executing the same solved policy, the BLM solved 102 tasks at 4.9 calls, and 112 at 0.76 calls with a thinking fallback. The same held on the other test sets (Appendix A). In other words, reading the solved policy can bring the model close to executing it in accuracy, but only at the full cost of re-deriving every turn.

Putting the decisions into the model’s weights is the other way to teach them. We fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on the 229 solved Opus conversations from which we measured the solved order’s turn counts. We evaluated it on test set 3, with a same-day rerun of the base model (Appendix D, not registered). The fine-tuned model solved 100 of 114 tasks at 17.6 model calls per conversation, against 109 at 1.5 for the BLM (−-7.9 points [−-15.8, −-0.9]). The base model, rerun the same day, solved 31 at 18.9. Section 10.1 compares the costs.

Observation 7: When the whole task is deciding, the solved policy needs little or no model. It beats every published method in inventory control, and in CI triage it costs about as much as the cheapest simple rule. In InventoryBench, with no model calls, the BLM scores 0.625, against 0.538 for the best published method, and it’s ahead on every batch (Table 5). On 60 instances drawn at random, it also beats Claude Opus 5.5 running the benchmark’s best published strategy, 0.598 against 0.560.

Better beliefs and a better decision rule contribute about equally (Figure 10). Feeding the BLM’s beliefs about demand and lead times into the published operations-research rule lifts it from 0.445 to 0.531. The solved decision rule then takes it to 0.611, and planning over beliefs to 0.625.

In CI triage the evidence is weaker. On the 169 failures with all retrigger outcomes observed, the controller cost $14.16 per failure. The cheapest simple rule on these failures, “retrigger once, then escalate”, cost $13.23, and so did Qwen3.8-27B given the same prices and probabilities. The difference from the rule isn’t significant (−-$1.32 to ++$3.22 per failure). Note that these failures aren’t a random sample: Mozilla had retriggered each of them at least twice. The controller is cheaper when we simulate the missing outcomes, but simulations can favor a controller, so we don’t count that as evidence (Appendix K).

Observation 8: Where the work is writing content, little can be solved in advance, and the agent’s own logs show this. In SymPy issue resolution the hard part is writing the patch. When we replayed the controller over the coding agent’s own runs, its state fixed the content of only 15 to 22% of its turns, its decidable share. These were mostly re-runs of a test the agent had already written. In telecom, the share is 98% of Opus’s turns and 76 to 80% of Qwen’s (Appendix G).

The outcome followed. On 21 issues, three runs each, the BLM with planning over beliefs solved 19 of 63, the same as a simple rule that stops the agent at its first passing test. It read and wrote 20% fewer tokens (127 thousand against 159 thousand per run). None of the solvers differed significantly in success from the agent on its own (14 of 63).

Figure 11 puts the domains on one plot: the decidable share, measured from the LLM agent’s own conversations, against the model calls the BLMs actually removed. Notice that telecom sits near the top right, SymPy near the bottom left, and InventoryBench in the corner, where the solved policy makes every decision.

7  Why BLMs work, and what still fails

Where do the gains of BLMs come from? Which solver should we use, what still fails, and where does calibration matter? This section takes them in turn.

Where the gains come from.

Table 4 takes a BLM apart on the 114 tasks of test set 2. Executing the solved policy with no LLM at all already solves 90 tasks. Letting Qwen3.8-27B write the turns the solved policy doesn’t cover brings this to 102, and letting it think on those turns brings it to 112.

It turns out that the order of the checks matters little: the order in the benchmark’s troubleshooting guide solves 103 tasks, a random order 97, and the solved order 102. In telecom, then, the gain doesn’t come from a better order. It comes from executing: asking for every relevant check, never forgetting one, and not handing the customer to a human while one remains (Observation 2). In InventoryBench it’s different. There the decision rule itself accounts for about half of the gain (Observation 7).

Which solver to use.

We ran three solvers in every domain, under the same states, probabilities and costs (Table 6). Which one did best followed what the moves do. When moves only buy information at a price, as retriggering a job does in CI, planning over beliefs was cheapest. QMDP assumes the uncertainty will be gone after one step, so it never pays for information. When information arrives anyway, as demand and deliveries do in InventoryBench, QMDP did well and planning over beliefs by rollout better.

When every move both tests for a fault and fixes it, as in telecom, the fixed order did as well as either. The one choice that did badly wherever it mattered was acting as if the most likely hidden state were certain.

What still fails.

Once we solve the decisions, the failures that remain are mostly in reading the conversation and carrying out steps. Each new telecom controller we built fixed the most common failure of the one before, and failures fell from 20 to 12 to 5 per 114 tasks.

Calibration matters near the thresholds.

Proposition 3 says that an estimate matters only near a decision threshold. CI shows the consequence (Figure 12). Without calibration, the controller’s most confident beliefs, where it backs out changes, were slightly too confident and fell on the wrong side of the threshold at which backing out pays. Calibrating the weight it gives each piece of evidence lowered its cost on the real test outcomes from $16.18 to $14.16 per failure (Table 11).

8  Building a BLM for a new workflow

How would you build a BLM for a workflow of your own? The recipe is short. Use the workflow’s own logs if you have them. If you don’t, generate data by running the agent. From the data, estimate the probability of each outcome and the cost of each move. Pose the decisions as a Markov decision process, solve it, and execute the solution around the model. The eight steps below say how. Each points to the result that supports it, and Table 7 (Appendix E) shows how each of our domains filled them in.

  1. 1.

    Make sure the work is mostly deciding. List the moves the agent makes again and again, and replay a first draft of the controller over the agent’s existing logs to measure the decidable share. If most turns are spent writing new content, as in our SymPy runs, a BLM will save little (Observation 8).

  2. 2.

    Keep in the state only what the decision needs (Observation 1). Start with the fields the system reports exactly, such as tool results and the checks already made, and read the rest of the text with simple rules. Split a state when its conversations keep needing different moves, and merge states that never do (Proposition 2).

  3. 3.

    Collect data until the decision states stop changing. If the last nn conversations added no new decision state, fewer than a share 3/n3/n of future conversations will reach a new one. Stop once that share is small enough, since those conversations fall back to the LLM (Section 4.3, Observation 1).

  4. 4.

    Count outcomes in the data, and let Bayes’ rule derive each state’s probabilities (Section 3.8). Where data are thin, start from an LLM’s own estimates, weighted like a fixed number of past tasks (Morita et al., 2008) (Observation 2). If an expert’s conversations exist, measure costs and probabilities from them, but don’t copy the expert’s choices (Table 1).

  5. 5.

    Price every move and outcome in one unit that whoever deploys the agent cares about, and spend precision only near the thresholds. Take the costs from what they pay or value (Section 3.6, Table 7). Calibrate the beliefs the controller acts on against real outcomes, near the thresholds where a decision flips (Proposition 3, Section 7).

  6. 6.

    Choose the solver by what the moves do. Plan over beliefs when moves only buy information. Use QMDP, improved by rollout, when information arrives anyway. Order the moves by probability per unit cost when each move both tests and fixes, which is exact when there’s one fault to find. And avoid acting as if the most likely hidden state were certain, as we found in Section 7.

  7. 7.

    Execute the moves the state fixes, and hand everything else to the LLM. Give the LLM the task’s own prompt and tools, read its turns back into the state, and block moves the state rules out, such as an early hand-off (Section 3.5, Observation 6).

  8. 8.

    Freeze the controller, test it on tasks it hasn’t seen, and fix what fails. Once you’ve solved the decisions, the failures that remain are in reading the conversation and carrying out steps. For example, in our telecom runs, two rounds of such fixes took failures from 20 to 5 per 114 tasks (Section 7).

Note that none of these steps changes the model. They need the agent’s logs, a reader and a solver, and the LLM keeps every turn the state doesn’t fix.

9  Related work

One question separates the work below from ours: who makes the agent’s decisions? A person can write them, a model can generate them from text, or a model can make them on every turn, or once and then reuse them. In a Bellman model, a solver computes them from estimated probabilities and stated costs.

Separating what a conversation’s state is from what to do next is an old idea in dialogue systems. Statistical dialogue managers tracked a belief over the user’s goal and planned each move with a partially observable Markov decision process (Williams and Young, 2007; Young et al., 2013). Hybrid Code Networks combined a learned model with action templates and domain code (Williams et al., 2017). We keep their split between tracking and deciding.

A second line of work puts structure around an LLM agent. Rasa’s CALM has an LLM turn each user message into commands that drive business flows written by developers (Bocklisch et al., 2024). NeMo Guardrails runs scripted or generated conversation flows (Rebedea et al., 2023), and StateFlow runs state machines designed by hand (Wu et al., 2024). NOMOS compiles written policies into gates on tool calls (Yu et al., 2026a), and PolicyGuide compiles them into workflow graphs that guide the agent (Kang et al., 2026). In these systems the flow or the rules are written by a person or generated from text.

Closest in machinery, Baheri and Wei (2026) estimate a Markov chain over abstract states from logs and solve it once, but only to block tool calls that lead to bad outcomes. The LLM still picks every move. In a BLM, we solve the decisions themselves, from estimated probabilities and stated costs.

FlowBench finds that workflow knowledge in the prompt helps agents plan but leaves much room for improvement (Xiao et al., 2024). A recent study finds that showing an agent its task state is unreliable. Enforcing the state helps when failures are frequent and the state can decide them, but hurts when the enforcement is wrong (Zhang et al., 2026). We find that executing a solved policy saves model calls, at similar or better accuracy, compared with describing it (Observation 6).

A third line turns an agent’s behavior into code or reusable plans. ABCAgent has a frontier model write the agent’s program, which then runs without the model (Qi et al., 2026). Agent just-in-time compilation has an LLM compile each task into code that is checked against the tools’ preconditions and postconditions (Winston et al., 2026). AgentJIT compiles recorded trajectories into guarded code that falls back to the LLM (AgentJIT Team, 2026). Another method compiles the steps that recur in a stronger model’s recorded reasoning into programs that guide a small model at every step (Bhat et al., 2026).

Workflow memory (Wang et al., 2025) and plan caching (Zhang et al., 2025b) reuse workflows or plans from earlier successful runs. These systems report gains in accuracy, speed or cost. In all of them a model makes the decisions, even when they’re reused. The decisions a BLM reuses are ones we solve from probabilities and costs.

Routers and cascades (Chen et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025; Aggarwal et al., 2024) reduce cost by choosing which model answers each query, sending easy queries to a cheaper one. A learned gate can also decide when a cheap agent should ask a stronger model for help. It works over a small set of abstract states, with values learned from task outcomes and a price per request (Sowietzki et al., 2026). It controls only that one choice, and the agent’s model still makes every move. These methods are complementary to BLMs: the turns a BLM hands to the LLM could be routed in the same way.

Other recent work changes how a language model is run, as we do, but so that it can read more rather than decide less. Recursive language models let the model call itself on pieces of an input too long for its context (Zhang et al., 2025a), and context language models let it rewrite its own context (Shao et al., 2026). Both change what the model reads, and the model still makes every decision. A BLM changes what the model decides: the turns the solved policy covers never reach it.

Other work trains the model itself. Agent-tuning work fine-tunes smaller models on trajectories from stronger ones (Zeng et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023). SCOPE-AD learns a cost-aware diagnostic strategy from Bellman targets and distills it into a Qwen model that acts as the agent (Yu et al., 2026b). In other words, both make each model call better. Section 10.1 compares this with running the solution outside the model.

Several methods help an LLM make expected-utility or information-seeking decisions (Liu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024; Ding et al., 2026). Each still calls the model at every decision, to supply the probabilities, the values of outcomes, or candidate questions from which it computes the choice, or to make the choice itself.

Work on decision calibration (Zhao et al., 2021; Kleinberg et al., 2023; Hu and Wu, 2024) judges predictions by the decisions they lead to, across classes of downstream tasks. Proposition 3 is the single-task case.

The theory we build on is classical. State abstraction (Li et al., 2006; Abel et al., 2016; Givan et al., 2003; Ferns et al., 2004) underlies Proposition 2, and its rule for splitting states is close to utile distinctions (McCallum, 1995). Ordering tests by probability per unit cost is a classical result in optimal search (Kadane and Simon, 1977) and the basis of decision-theoretic troubleshooting (Heckerman et al., 1995), and inventory control has strong operations-research and learning baselines (Arrow et al., 1951; Xin, 2021; Gijsbrechts et al., 2022).

Work on continuous integration selects which tests to run (Memon et al., 2017; Machalica et al., 2019), and work on flaky tests studies why they fail (Luo et al., 2014; Parry et al., 2022) and detects or ranks flaky tests and intermittent failures (Kowalczyk et al., 2020; Lampel et al., 2021). Note that we decide what to do about a failure, under explicit costs. The agent benchmarks we use are τ2\tau^{2}-bench (Barres et al., 2026), which extends τ\tau-bench (Yao et al., 2025), SymPy issues from SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024), and InventoryBench (Baek et al., 2026).

10  Discussion

Three questions remain. How does solving once compare with training the model on the same data? What does a Bellman model look like to someone who knows compilers? And what does the decision process give up?

10.1  Solving once versus training

The obvious alternative to a BLM is to train the model on the same data: fine-tune a small model on a stronger model’s conversations, or on the workflow’s own logs. Training and solving have the same shape. Both pay a cost once and recover it over many conversations. They differ in what that cost pays for.

Concretely, training changes how the model decides on every turn. Solving takes the turns away from the model. A fine-tuned agent still calls its model on every turn, so its cost per conversation and its response time stay those of the model it runs on. Observation 6 shows both sides on the same tasks. Trained on Opus’s conversations, Qwen3.8-27B learned much of what Opus does well, going from 31 to 100 of 114 tasks. But it still made 17.6 model calls per conversation, against 1.5 for the BLM.

The one-time costs differ as well. Fine-tuning Qwen3.8-27B on 207 of the 229 conversations (we held out 22 to choose the epoch) took 4.4 hours on one H200 GPU. Any change to the data, the written policy or the base model means training again. Solving the decision process is arithmetic. In telecom, for example, it amounts to ordering fourteen checks.

Building a BLM costs something else, the work of writing its readers, templates and the code for its procedures. Proposition 4 gives the point at which that pays off. With Opus on test set 3, the BLM saved $0.48 per conversation ($0.012 against $0.49 for Opus alone). So a controller that costs BB to build pays for itself after B/0.48B/0.48 conversations: about 210 conversations for a build that costs $100, and 2,100 for one that costs $1,000.

Some properties of a solved policy don’t depend on how accurate the agent is, and training doesn’t provide them:

  • •

    When we solve the decision process exactly, the solved policy is optimal for the estimates, and Propositions 1 and 2 bound what discretizing costs. A trained model comes with no such statement.

  • •

    We can read the solved policy decision by decision (Table 1) and test it against a specification. Trained weights can’t.

  • •

    Probabilities and costs are separate inputs, so we handle a change in costs by solving again, with no new data. A trained model needs training again.

  • •

    We can measure how much the solved policy will save from existing logs, before deploying it (Section 4.5).

The two aren’t exclusive. We can use a fine-tuned model as a BLM’s fallback, writing the turns the solved policy doesn’t cover.

An analogy with compilers.

Readers who know compilers will recognize the arrangement. An LLM agent is an interpreter: it holds its decisions implicitly, in a model and a prompt, and carries it out by re-deriving each decision as it goes. Discretize, Then Decide compiles the decisions that recur. Like a tracing just-in-time compiler (Gal et al., 2009), it compiles only the paths that come back again and again, and guards each one. When a guard fails, it falls back to the interpreter, a step known as deoptimization (Hölzle et al., 1992). The analogy also says where the savings stop: what never comes back stays interpreted, which is the limit of Section 4.5.

10.2  What the decision process gives up, and why the LLM stays

Any way of choosing among recurring moves that separates what’s believed from what’s wanted, and picks the move with the best expected outcome, is a decision process. Given the estimates, solving it exactly loses nothing. What can be lost is what that form assumes. The states must summarize the part of the history that matters.

Expected cost ignores limits on other costs and on risk, which decision processes with constraints handle by limiting expected costs (Altman, 1999). Rules that must always hold can be enforced by removing the moves that break them. A solved policy is also fixed, so people who deal with the agent often could learn how it decides, and exploit that. And a frozen solved policy stops learning, which posterior sampling addresses (Osband et al., 2013).

One limit we can’t handle this way. A solver chooses only among moves that someone listed, and only the LLM can invent a new one. When the LLM keeps handling some state in a new way that works, that way becomes a candidate move for the next version of the solved policy. This is why the LLM stays in the loop: it handles what’s new, and shows what we should solve next.

11  Limitations and future work

Where might these results not carry over? Our strongest evidence comes from one benchmark generator. τ2\tau^{2}-bench’s telecom tasks combine 19 fault types, and LLMs simulate its customers.
