Test sets drawn at random after we froze each controller protect against choosing tasks that favor the controller, not against a different generator. And the telecom results are one attempt per task except on unseen-fault set 2.

The other domains meet a lower standard (Section 5.3 and Observation 7). In InventoryBench, we developed the controller’s demand forecasts and its rollout while looking at results on the whole benchmark. On two retail benchmarks, where the agent alone already solved most tasks, our controllers gained nothing (Appendix A).

A coding agent wrote the controllers under our direction (Section 3.10), and we haven’t tested a controller built from the recipe of Section 8 alone. We applied the stopping rule of Section 4.3 after collecting the training data, rather than using it to decide how many to collect.

Four directions follow. The first is how to discretize optimally. Choosing the states is an optimization problem of its own: fewer facts make the states repeat sooner but can merge conversations that need different moves, and more facts do the opposite. Proposition 2 bounds what a given choice of states costs, and the split-and-merge rule of Section 8 improves one, but neither finds the best.

The second is to build controllers from the recipe alone, by a coding agent with no person in the loop, which would show what a controller costs to build. The third is to add finished conversations back into the counts, so that a deployed solved policy keeps learning. Last, a solved policy is a finite object, so we can test it against a specification. For example, we can count in what share of states it makes an important move without a person, as is done for access-control rules (Eiers et al., 2022). We pursue this separately.

12  Conclusion

An agent in a bounded workflow keeps meeting the same states, and an LLM agent re-derives each of them whenever it meets them. Discretize, Then Decide treats those decisions as an optimization problem, solves it once from the workflow’s own data, and leaves the model only what the states don’t cover.

In telecom support this brought a small open model within one task of a frontier model at 93% fewer model calls, and let the frontier model drop almost all of its calls. In inventory control, a solved policy that calls no model beat every published method. Where the work is writing rather than deciding, the agent’s own logs show that there’s little to gain. Much of what agents do in bounded workflows is deciding, and deciding can be solved once.

Appendix A Registrations and their outcomes

This appendix lists every registration we made and its outcome, including targets that were missed and forecasts that were wrong. Seven registrations are in a public GitHub repository, https://github.com/adarsh-vatsa/dtd-preregistration. Each commit holds the analysis plan, any forecasts, and the frozen files or their SHA-256 hashes, and, where tasks were drawn, the public random number used for the draw and the drawn tasks. GitHub’s push records confirm the commit times given below. The other registrations were recorded locally before their runs.

In the repository, the three telecom controllers are named v5c, v5e and v5f, test sets 1 to 3 are draws 1 to 3, and the unseen-fault sets are holdouts. Intervals are 95% intervals from resampling tasks, in points of success rate. Cost forecast errors are (forecast −- actual)/actual.

The 495 telecom test tasks were held in reserve and drawn in turn. A first set of 114, which we call test set 0, served an earlier controller that the body doesn’t report (below). It took all four of the reserve’s no-service tasks, 36 mobile-data tasks and 74 picture-messaging tasks. Test set 1 took the 34 mobile-data tasks that remained and 80 picture-messaging tasks, which left only picture-messaging tasks for test sets 2 and 3. Test set 3 was drawn from the 153 tasks left after test sets 0 to 2. Unseen-fault set 1 was drawn from all 501 unseen-fault tasks, and unseen-fault set 2 from the 441 left after it.

The telecom results

  • •

    Test set 1 and unseen-fault set 1, first controller (public; commit e969d50). On both sets we compared Qwen3.8-27B alone against Qwen3.8-27B as a BLM under each of the three solvers. On test set 1 we also compared Claude Opus 5.5 alone against Opus as a BLM (fixed order). Primary comparison, Qwen as a BLM against Qwen alone on test set 1: ++36.8 points [27.2, 46.5], met. Stated target, Opus alone’s level: not met, −-14.9 [−-22.8, −-7.0]. On unseen-fault set 1, ++33.3 [16.7, 50.0]. QMDP and planning over beliefs against Qwen alone: ++29.8 and ++31.6 on test set 1, ++26.7 and ++18.3 on unseen-fault set 1.

    The random number used for the draw was published 47 s before the controller’s files were hashed, and the runs started 28 s before the registration was committed. Conversations that ended in an infrastructure error, with no outcome, were rerun once with the same code (84 of the 114 for Opus alone and 17 for Opus as a BLM). No rerun rule had been registered.

  • •

    Test set 2, second controller (public; b0163d9). The same comparisons as on test set 1. Primary comparison, Qwen as a BLM within 5 points of Opus alone: not met, −-7.9 [−-14.9, −-1.8]. Against Qwen alone: ++62.3 with the fixed order, ++60.5 with QMDP and ++54.4 with planning over beliefs. Opus as a BLM against Opus alone: ++1.8 [−-1.8, 5.3].

    The registration gives as its reason that one flaw of the first controller caused 16 of its 19 failures. That count was taken before the run had finished, and the final count is 11 of 20. The first random number we took was 3 s older than the freeze, so before any test ran the tasks were drawn again from one published two minutes later, as the registration records. As on test set 1, conversations without an outcome were rerun (87 of Opus alone’s 114), and three Qwen runs were moved to another machine during the run.

  • •

    Test set 2 with Claude Opus 5.5 as the customer, second controller (public; 99f62aa). Registered after an unregistered trial on the first 50 tasks of test set 2, which supplied the forecast. The other 64 tasks are the confirmatory set: their outcomes with the Qwen customer were known, and none with the Opus customer. Primary comparison met: Qwen as a BLM solved 63 of 64 against 45 alone, ++28.1 [17.2, 40.6], against a forecast of ++28 (forecast success about 95% and 72%, realized 98% and 70%), at 1.6 calls per conversation against 19.9 (forecast below 2 and above 15).

    On all 114 tasks, Opus alone and Opus as a BLM each solved 114, at 17.1 and 0.68 calls per conversation. The forecast, within 3 points of Opus alone with fewer than 1.5 calls, was met. Qwen with thinking solved 103, and Qwen with thinking and the checklist solved 114, at 17.3 calls. Some comparisons were started early or resumed at higher concurrency to use free machines, and two conversations cut off by an outage were rerun once. Code and settings didn’t change.

  • •

    Test set 3, third controller (public; 51db041). Built after studying the second controller’s failures on test sets 1 and 2 and on training conversations. It was frozen at 19:58:29 UTC on 9 October 2026, and the tasks were drawn with the first published random number at least 60 s later (20:00:00). The registration was committed at 20:00:40, and the runs started at 20:00:51. We compared Qwen alone, Qwen as a BLM under each solver and with a thinking fallback, Qwen with thinking and the checklist, and Opus alone and as a BLM. Primary comparison met: Qwen as a BLM solved 109 of 114 against 33 alone, ++66.7 [57.0, 75.4].

    Targets, all met. Qwen as a BLM came within 5 points of Opus alone, which solved 110 (−-0.9 [−-6.1, 4.4]). The thinking fallback came within 2 points (110 solved, 0.0 [−-4.4, 4.4]). Qwen and Opus as BLMs made fewer than 2 and 1 calls per conversation (1.47 and 0.25). QMDP solved 112, planning over beliefs 111, Opus as a BLM 112, and Qwen with thinking and the checklist 105, at 19.1 calls (no forecast). The forecasts, each followed by its outcome, were Qwen alone 25–35% (29%), Qwen as a BLM about 106 (109), the thinking fallback about 110 (110), Opus alone about 111 (110) and Opus as a BLM about 113 (112). QMDP and planning over beliefs were forecast within 5 points of the fixed order (met: ++2.6 and ++1.8).

    Customer messages per conversation: 30.0 (Qwen alone), 33.7 (fixed order), 30.9 (QMDP), 31.7 (planning over beliefs), 31.4 (thinking fallback), 28.2 (Opus alone) and 31.5 (Opus as a BLM). Failures: 5 for Qwen as a BLM, 4 for the thinking fallback, 4 for Opus alone and 2 for Opus as a BLM. No conversation ended in an infrastructure error.

  • •

    Unseen-fault set 2, third controller, with Opus as the customer and three attempts per task (public; b66bcdb). Registered after the primary test set 3 results, with the third controller unchanged. The files were hashed at 22:56:39 UTC on 9 October, and the 60 tasks were drawn with the first published random number at least 60 s later (22:58:00). The registration was committed at 22:58:39, and the runs started at 22:58:43. We compared Qwen alone, Qwen as a BLM with thinking off and with a thinking fallback, Opus alone, and Opus as a BLM. Primary comparison met: on the share of attempts solved, Qwen as a BLM 97.8% against 67.2% alone, ++30.6 [22.8, 38.9].

    Targets. The pass3 of Qwen as a BLM was at least 25 points above Qwen alone’s, as targeted (93.3% against 40.0%, ++53.3 [41.7, 66.7]). Qwen and Opus as BLMs made fewer than 2.5 and 1 calls per conversation, as targeted (0.97 and 0.27). Two targets, Qwen as a BLM within 5 points of Opus alone and the thinking fallback within 3 points, weren’t evaluated as registered, because Opus alone was stopped after 41 of its 180 attempts to limit cost. It solved all 41, and further attempts could only have lowered its rate, so stopping early couldn’t have favored these two targets. The thinking fallback and Opus as a BLM solved all 180 attempts, at 0.32 and 0.27 calls per conversation.

    The forecasts, each followed by its outcome, were Qwen alone 55–70% of attempts (67.2%), Qwen as a BLM about 95% (97.8%), the thinking fallback about 96% (100%), Opus alone about 97% (41 of 41 attempts run) and Opus as a BLM about 98% (100%). We also forecast pass3 5 to 15 points below pass1 for Qwen alone (missed: 27 points below), and 0 to 6 points below as a BLM (met: 4.5 for Qwen as a BLM, 0 for the others). Customer messages per conversation: 28.4 (Qwen alone), 31.4 (Qwen as a BLM) and 29.8 (thinking fallback). The Opus service, which played the customer, was down for about a day during the runs. As registered, attempts that ended in an infrastructure error were rerun once with the same code: 128, 112, 107 and 131 of 180 for Qwen alone, Qwen as a BLM, the thinking fallback and Opus as a BLM. Opus alone was stopped after 12 of its 151.

While four comparisons on test set 2 were running, before any had finished, we fixed in writing (9 October 2026, 16:15 UTC) how the paper would be framed. The four were Qwen with the checklist, with thinking, with thinking and the checklist, and with the oracle plan. If the best of them solved fewer than 67 of the 114 tasks, halfway between Qwen alone (31) and Qwen as a BLM (102), the paper would lead with the difference between knowing a solved policy and executing it. Otherwise it would lead with cost and report the telecom accuracy gain as a decomposition. The oracle plan solved 106, so the paper leads with cost.

The other domains

  • •

    InventoryBench, Claude Opus 5.5 baseline (local, no forecast). The plan, the harness and the primary comparison were hashed before any run. The comparison is the BLM as reported against Opus running the benchmark’s best published strategy, in which the LLM sets each order after seeing the operations-research rule’s recommendation, paired over 60 instances. Result: 0.598 against 0.560, a difference of ++0.038 [0.016, 0.062]. Against Opus running the benchmark’s LLM-only agent, it was 0.598 against 0.559.

    NIST’s public random numbers had stopped for five hours, so after a dated amendment the 60 instances were drawn from the first number published by drand, the League of Entropy’s public random numbers. An earlier draw from an old NIST number was discarded unused. The benchmark’s agent scripts ran unchanged, except that their API client pointed to our endpoints and SciPy’s normal quantile came from an equivalent function in Python’s standard library. Fifteen Opus runs were run again in full. Seven were cut short by a network outage, and eight never finished because the benchmark’s own log extractor failed, after which we added a guard (no decision on a log that can’t be parsed). Before any comparison finished, we changed the scoring script to read the published results’ file paths and to compute the pre-specified paired interval. The analysis didn’t change.

  • •

    SymPy (local, no forecast). A first test was withdrawn because of a bug: the decision table, fitted again, put every state under one merged issue type, while the controller looked states up under each issue’s own type. After the fix, two versions were frozen before any run: the fixed controller, and a variant in which every solver defers to the agent when its two best moves are close. Both were tested on the withdrawn test’s 21 issues, three runs each.

    Fixed controller: planning over beliefs solved 19 of 63, the most-likely-state solver 17 and QMDP 16, against 14 for the agent alone and 19 for the rule that stops at the first passing test. The most-likely-state and planning controllers mostly tell the agent to run a test before its first edit, QMDP mostly defers to it, and all three end most runs by executing the submission. Variant: most-likely-state 16, QMDP 18, planning over beliefs 15. No controller’s success differs significantly from the agent alone’s (every interval includes or touches zero), and every controller’s token saving is significant. One fact the controller reads is whether the agent’s script that reproduces the issue passes. On pilot runs, a pass was wrong a third of the time (15 of 45).

  • •

    CI triage (two public registrations; 607ba1e and its amendment 6cc735b). The controller we report and the recalibrated controller (Table 11) were each hashed before their single scoring run on the test window, and registered afterwards, in the amendment. The hashed file of the first was later edited in place into the second, so its hash record and its results remain, but the file doesn’t. The two registrations also forecast the cost per failure on failures from 7 October 2026 on, which hadn’t been collected or viewed when each was registered. The first, for the simpler controller, forecast $8.15 against $13.18 for the best rule, both computed on the failures its model was fitted on. The second forecast $9.51 for the recalibrated controller (range $7.14–11.89), its score on the test window. These forecasts are scored after 23 October 2026 and aren’t part of this paper.

Registrations not reported in the body

  • •

    An earlier telecom controller that only blocked hand-offs (local). Tested on the benchmark’s 114 base tasks, two attempts each, and on test set 0. Against a controller that only executed account lookups: ++13.6 points [7.0, 20.2], against a forecast of ++10.5, which met the registration’s second criterion, that the forecast fall within the realized interval. The forecast put none of the gain on mobile-data tasks, where the realized gain was 15.3 points. Against Qwen alone: ++11.8 [3.9, 19.3] on the base tasks and ++20.2 [10.5, 29.8] on test set 0. Against a simpler rule taken from the written policy, which blocks every hand-off unless the reader sees a reason in the written policy for it, such as a locked SIM card: −-3.1 [−-9.6, 3.5], so no better.

    The token forecast missed: ++32,103 billed tokens per conversation, agent and simulated customer together, against ++18,375. Test set 0 was drawn with a random number published 78 s before the controller’s file was frozen, and a later, unregistered controller was also evaluated on it.

  • •

    SymPy, an earlier controller that suggested or executed stops (local; 20 issues, three runs each). When the controller only suggested stopping, the agent followed 6.5% of the suggestions, and the saving fell short of its forecast (9.1% against 42.4%). A version that executed the stop, added by a written addendum before its runs, cut billed tokens by 36.5%, at 40.0% against 43.3% success (interval −-18.3 to ++10.0). Of the saving, 54.6% came from 12 runs that gave up at the first step.

  • •

    τ\tau-bench retail, a different benchmark from τ2\tau^{2}-bench retail (local; 115 tasks, two attempts each). No controller differed from the agent alone (61.7% against 60.0%, interval −-5.7 to ++9.1). The success forecast missed by 9.4 points and the cost forecast by −-16.6%. The forecast for the agent alone was written after it ran.

  • •

    τ2\tau^{2}-bench retail (local, no forecast). It was frozen at 13:24:48 UTC on 8 October 2026, and the runs began 7 s later, on the 40 unused test tasks, two attempts each. The agent alone solved 66 of 80; as BLMs, the most-likely-state solver solved 61, QMDP 66 and planning over beliefs 66. This controller left the matching of items, variants and payment methods to the LLM, and the agent alone already solved most tasks, which left little room for a gain.

  • •

    Checks of two fitted models before evaluation (local). A simulated SymPy world predicted the agent’s success and cost on held-out issues (0.385 against 0.400; cost ++0.2%), but failed its calibration and Markov-structure criteria. The final τ\tau-bench retail decision table predicted the agent’s success and cost (0.636 against 0.600; cost −-1.2%), but failed 3 of its 5 criteria before any controller run.

Appendix B Proofs

Proposition 2.

Write A⋆​(s,a)=Q⋆​(s,a)−V⋆​(s)≥0A^{\star}(s,a)=Q^{\star}(s,a)-V^{\star}(s)\geq 0, with V⋆=0V^{\star}=0 once the task has ended. If 𝔼π​[T]\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[T] is infinite the bound is vacuous, so let 𝔼π​[T]<∞\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[T]<\infty; then telescoping ∑t<T[c⁡(st,at)+V⋆​(st+1)−V⋆​(st)]\sum_{t<T}[c(s_{t},a_{t})+V^{\star}(s_{t+1})-V^{\star}(s_{t})] and taking expectations gives the performance difference lemma (Kakade and Langford, 2002) in its undiscounted form, Vπ​(s0)−V⋆​(s0)=𝔼π​[∑t<TA⋆​(st,at)]V^{\pi}(s_{0})-V^{\star}(s_{0})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\big[\sum_{t<T}A^{\star}(s_{t},a_{t})\big]. Let ss lie in decision state zz, let Q¯​(z,a)=∑s′∈zw⁡(s′)​Q⋆​(s′,a)\bar{Q}(z,a)=\sum_{s^{\prime}\in z}w(s^{\prime})Q^{\star}(s^{\prime},a) for weights ww on zz, and let a^=arg⁡mina​Q¯​(z,a)\hat{a}=\arg\min_{a}\bar{Q}(z,a). By ε\varepsilon-consistency |Q⋆​(s,a)−Q¯​(z,a)|≤ε|Q^{\star}(s,a)-\bar{Q}(z,a)|\leq\varepsilon for every aa, so Q⋆​(s,a^)≤Q¯​(z,a^)+ε≤Q¯​(z,a⋆​(s))+ε≤Q⋆​(s,a⋆​(s))+2​εQ^{\star}(s,\hat{a})\leq\bar{Q}(z,\hat{a})+\varepsilon\leq\bar{Q}(z,a^{\star}(s))+\varepsilon\leq Q^{\star}(s,a^{\star}(s))+2\varepsilon, that is, A⋆​(s,a^)≤2​εA^{\star}(s,\hat{a})\leq 2\varepsilon at every state. Summing over the TT decisions gives the bound. □\square

Proposition 3.

With a^=a⋆​(b^)\hat{a}=a^{\star}(\hat{b}) and a=a⋆​(b)a=a^{\star}(b), C⁡(a^,b)−C⁡(a,b)=[C⁡(a^,b)−C⁡(a^,b^)]+[C⁡(a^,b^)−C⁡(a,b^)]+[C⁡(a,b^)−C⁡(a,b)]≤(b−b^)​sa^+0+(b^−b)​sa≤|b^−b|​maxa,a′​|sa−sa′|C(\hat{a},b)-C(a,b)=[C(\hat{a},b)-C(\hat{a},\hat{b})]+[C(\hat{a},\hat{b})-C(a,\hat{b})]+[C(a,\hat{b})-C(a,b)]\leq(b-\hat{b})s_{\hat{a}}+0+(\hat{b}-b)s_{a}\leq|\hat{b}-b|\max_{a,a^{\prime}}|s_{a}-s_{a^{\prime}}|. If no threshold separates the beliefs, a^=a\hat{a}=a.

Appendix C Models and settings

Qwen3.8-27B is served with vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) at temperature 0 with thinking off, unless stated. With thinking on, we use the model’s recommended sampling (temperature 0.6, top-pp 0.95). In SymPy, the coding agent samples at temperature 0.6 with thinking off, so its three runs on each issue differ.

Claude Opus 5.5 is reached through Claude Code’s command-line interface, behind an adapter that makes it behave like an ordinary chat model. The benchmark’s prompt replaces the interface’s system prompt, the interface’s own tools are turned off, and tool calls are written as text. The interface’s default reasoning is kept: 61% of the Opus-alone agent calls on test sets 1–3 used thinking tokens. The interface adds a fixed overhead to every Opus call: a minimal call through it, with a one-word reply, took 2.6 s (measured with Claude Sonnet 5.5). So a native interface would cut the waiting times we report for Opus alone, but not remove them. In telecom, the simulated customer is Qwen3.8-27B at temperature 0, except in the replications where Claude Opus 5.5 plays the customer.

Appendix D The fine-tuning baseline

We fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on the same conversations from which the solved order’s turn counts were measured: the 229 solved Claude Opus 5.5 conversations on training tasks. Each conversation was rebuilt exactly as the agent saw it: the benchmark’s own system prompt and tool definitions, the customer’s messages, and the agent’s messages, tool calls and tool results. The customer’s own actions on the phone aren’t visible to the agent, so we left them out.

We held out 22 conversations to choose the epoch and trained on 207. Training used LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) with rank 16 on the attention, linear-attention and MLP projections, which gives 108.8 million trainable parameters (0.40% of the model). We used AdamW at a learning rate of 10−410^{-4} with cosine decay, eight conversations per update and three epochs, with the loss on the agent’s turns only and thinking off, as at evaluation. It ran on one H200 GPU. The fine-tuned model was evaluated on test set 3 with the same harness and settings as the registered Qwen-alone arm, with a same-day rerun of the base model as a control. This comparison wasn’t registered.

Training took 4 hours 25 minutes on the GPU, including validation and merging the adapter into the model. The third epoch had the lowest validation loss (0.342) and is the one evaluated. On test set 3 it solved 100 of 114 tasks, at 17.6 model calls and 163 thousand agent tokens per conversation. The base model, rerun the same day, solved 31 at 18.9 calls and 184 thousand tokens (the registered run solved 33).

Appendix E How each domain fills in the decision problem

For each domain, Table 7 lists what the state holds, what’s hidden and where its prior comes from, and how text or data is read into the state. It also lists the moves, the cost unit, and how each of the three solvers is implemented.

Appendix F The Bellman model’s conversation, turn by turn

Table 8 follows the BLM’s conversation of Figure 6 from the controller’s side. At every turn, the controller reads what came in, updates the state, and sends the move the solved policy picks if the state fixes its content. Here it always did. The customer’s first message set the kind of problem, and a template asked for the phone number. The controller then looked up the account, the line and the plan, reading each tool call’s arguments from the previous result. It sent the checks in the solved order, one template each, and read every reply. A refusal to do two things at once got a re-ask. “Yes, I’m currently abroad in France” set off the roaming procedure, an executed tool call followed by an instruction. And “It’s working now!” ended the conversation with a closing template. The model was never called.

Appendix G The decidable share

We replay a frozen controller over the conversations of the LLM agent on its own. The controller receives the customer’s messages and the agent’s own tool results as the agent saw them, and at each of the agent’s turns it’s asked, on a copy of its state, what it would do.

A turn is templatable if the controller’s state fixes its content, so that a controller could send it without a model. This is the measure we report. In telecom, it’s a move from the controller’s executable menu in that state. In SymPy, it’s a submission or a re-run of a test the agent has already written, although our SymPy controller executes only the submission. A turn agrees if it’s exactly the controller’s next move, and is anticipated if the controller had any move ready (since a move not yet made stays proposed turn after turn, this counts loosely).

As a check, the same replay over the BLM’s own conversations reproduces which turns the controller executed on all 9,227 turns of test sets 2 and 3. For test set 1, which the first controller ran, we replay the second controller; replaying the third instead changes no share by more than 6.4 points.

Table 9 gives the shares. The controller’s state fixes nearly all of Opus’s turns in telecom, and a small share of the SymPy agent’s turns.

Appendix H Measuring saturation

We replayed every conversation on a telecom training task that ran without a solved policy through the controller’s frozen reader, in the order the conversations were collected (7 to 8 October 2026, UTC). There are 1,721 such conversations on 750 distinct tasks, with 29,264 agent turns: 590 from Qwen3.8-27B on its own, 731 from Qwen3.8-27B exploration runs, and 400 from Claude Opus 5.5 on its own. By kind of problem, 848 are picture messaging, 794 mobile data and 79 no service. In the exploration runs an earlier controller executed the account lookups (15.6% of their turns) and blocked some hand-offs at random. The LLM chose every other move.

As a check, we used three test runs in which the reader logged its state while the LLM agent worked on its own. They were Qwen3.8-27B on test set 3 and on unseen-fault set 2, and Qwen3.8-27B with thinking and the checklist on test set 3. On all 7,998 of their turns, the replay reproduces the logged state.

We counted four things at every agent turn. The decision state is the kind of problem, whether it’s fixed yet, anything stopping a fix, and the first check in the solved order not yet made: 69 distinct values, the last first seen at conversation 1,542. A simpler state that keeps only how many relevant checks remain (counted up to three) took 36 of its 108 possible values, the last at conversation 1,305, and that value was a misreading by the reader. It saturates partly by construction, because 96.7% of turns fall in the “three or more” group.

The record of checks adds the full set of checks made so far: 2,664 values, with new ones to the end. The messages are the agent’s texts, lowercased, with digits, identifiers and phone numbers masked: 18,254 distinct among 22,538 text turns. Over 200 random orders of the conversations, the median number of conversations since the last new decision state was 176 (95% range 18 to 677), so the observed 179 is typical rather than an artifact of the order of collection.

Table 10 gives, for each test set, how many conversations of the LLM on its own reached a decision state, or a record of checks, not seen in training. Besides the accuracy figures of Section 3.8, the reader identified anything stopping a fix in 1,716 of the 1,721 training conversations, and most of its errors on whether it was fixed read a failure as fixed.

Three caveats apply. About half of the training conversations concern mobile data, while test sets 2 and 3 and both unseen-fault sets are all picture messaging. Saturation is measured on the reader’s states, not on the true state of the phone. And agents that behave differently from those in the training data reach unseen states more often: Qwen3.8-27B with the checklist and thinking did so in 24 of the 114 conversations of test set 2.

Appendix I Success by number of faults

On every telecom test set, Qwen3.8-27B on its own does worse as the number of faults in a task grows, and as a Bellman model, it drops much less (Figure 13).

Appendix J A simulated world for comparing decisions

To compare an LLM’s decisions with optimal ones exactly, we used a simulated world of a coding agent with hidden variables, in which the expected cost of any controller can be computed. It has 46 reachable states. An LLM given a one-page description of the task estimated, in one pass, the probabilities of each move’s outcomes. We solved the decision process over the observed state twice, once with those estimates and once with the true probabilities. This solver is a table found by dynamic programming, and it doesn’t track the hidden variables. Both tables cost 29.94 minutes per task.

Asked instead to choose the move in each state, the LLM cost 32.96 minutes per task with a quick judgment and 32.21 after reasoning about what each move would reveal. Its choices agreed with the true-probability table’s in 54% and 59% of states. A controller that knows the hidden state costs 18.82.

The solvers compare as in the real domains. Tracking a belief about the hidden variables helps: QMDP costs 27.9 minutes per task, less than the table’s 29.94. Looking further ahead adds nothing (27.89 to 27.96 for horizons 1 to 6), and acting as if the most likely hidden state were certain loops (238.8). The controller that knows the hidden state is out of reach because no available move reveals the remaining information.

The LLM roles were played by Claude subagents given only the task description. The one-pass estimates and the quick judgments came from Claude Opus 5.5, and the reasoned choices from an earlier model, Claude Opus 5, so the gap to those choices may be too large. The world, including its probabilities, was written by Claude, and its list of states was designed to be sufficient, so this experiment shows what an LLM does with a well-posed decision problem, not how well one can be posed.

Appendix K CI triage in detail

Prices come from published runner list prices ($0.006 per minute on Linux, $0.010 on Windows, $0.062 on macOS) and a developer’s time at $64.44 per hour. Take the costs of Section 5.1, once no retrigger is worth its price. Marking a failure intermittent is the cheapest final move when the belief bb that it’s a regression is below 0.125, since two developer-hours times bb is then less than fifteen minutes. Backing out is the cheapest above 0.75, since one developer-hour times 1−b1-b is then less than fifteen minutes, and escalating is the cheapest in between.

The controller we report plans two moves ahead over bb. Its prior comes from a logistic model of the failing test’s label history and the change that triggered it. It treats retriggers of the same failure as correlated, with a flakiness rate for each test. And the weight it gives each piece of evidence is calibrated on failures from the training window. Table 11 also scores three variants. The first is the same controller without that calibration. The second uses the same models with a different calibration, which recalibrates the belief itself on training-window failures with observed retrigger outcomes. The third is a simpler controller with an outcome model that treats retriggers as independent and gives every test in a suite one flakiness rate.

Table 11 scores each method three ways. The first column uses only the 169 test failures with all retriggers observed, so nothing is simulated. Mozilla retriggered each of these at least twice, so they aren’t a random sample, and staff labels may reflect the retrigger results. The other two columns score all 1,173 test failures. For the 1,004 of them (86%) with some retrigger outcomes unobserved, the missing outcomes are simulated, either from a pass rate per test fitted on all the data or from the simpler controller’s outcome model. On real outcomes, the controller we report and “retrigger once, then escalate” differ by −-$1.32 to ++$3.22 per failure (95% interval, controller minus rule).

The controller without calibration shows how a simulator can favor a controller when the two share an outcome model. It is the most expensive of the four planning controllers on real outcomes, yet the cheapest of all in the simulator that shares its per-test model.

Two further simulators share no controller’s model. Both are fitted on training outcomes, one with a retrigger pass rate per label, and one with a pass rate per label and previous outcome. With every controller fitted again on more training data, the controller without calibration was again the cheapest ($9.02 and $8.47 per failure). The design we report cost $9.40 and $9.17, which is 25% and 22% less than the best alternative, Qwen given prices and probabilities ($12.56 and $11.69). And the recalibrated controller was cheaper than every rule, both Qwen controllers, QMDP and the most-likely-label solver in all four simulators (paired 95% intervals below zero).

Given the same prices and probabilities as the controller, Qwen3.8-27B retriggered first on 612 of 631 failures of a development sample, and Claude Opus 5.5 on 541. Asked to read a failure’s error lines, Opus was right 80.0% of the time and Qwen 73.4%, against 62.0% for always answering “intermittent”.
